transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. ____. What brings you in today?

Hi. Well, I'm here because... I keep leaving my station at work. Or I'll just pop up during meetings when I'm supposed to stay put on the floor. My supervisor told me it's becoming a safety problem, because I just take off before I even really think about it. So, that's what brought me in.
Do you also have trouble staying focused on tasks or following through on instructions?

Yeah, I do. Like, when I have to do the inventory logs or read through the CNC training pages... I start out really trying to pay attention, but after just a few minutes, the numbers or words just kind of blur together. I have to keep going back and starting over because I realize I didn't actually take any of it in.
Did you have problems like this when you were a child?

Yeah, I did. Even back in elementary school... I was always the kid who just couldn't stay in my seat. I'd talk over the teacher a lot, and my parents were always getting notes sent home because I would just blurt things out or start wandering around the room. So, yeah, it's been going on since I was little.
When you’re told to stay in your seat or follow instructions at work, do you usually feel angry or resentful about it?

No, I don't really get mad about it. I mean, I know why the rules are there, especially on the floor with the machines and everything. It's not that I'm trying to be difficult or rebellious. It's just... I do it before I even think. Like, my body just gets up and goes. I actually feel pretty bad when my supervisor has to get onto me, because I want to do it right, I just... I can't seem to stop myself from moving in the moment.

latest_inference.note: Ruled out oppositional/defiant pattern and most personality/impulse-control alternatives based on childhood onset, pervasive inattention/hyperactivity, and lack of anger or deliberate rule-breaking. final_diagnosis.reason: The interview supports attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive presentation, with symptoms beginning in childhood and persisting into adulthood. He reports leaving his workstation impulsively, difficulty staying seated, blurting out, talking over teachers, and distractibility with tasks, causing occupational safety and performance problems. There is no evidence that the behavior is driven by oppositionality or anger.
